note: Matthew's blessings are in the third person and spiritual: {mt 5:3 οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι} (“the poor **in spirit**”), {mt 5:6 πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην} (“hungering for **righteousness**”). Luke's are second person, direct and material: {lk 6:20 Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοί} (“blessed are **you** poor”), {lk 6:21 οἱ πεινῶντες νῦν} (“you who hunger **now**”). Which is closer to the original is one of the classic questions in Gospel study.

Only Luke follows his blessings with matching curses, so that each beatitude has its mirror image: {lk 6:24 οὐαὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις} (“woe to you who are rich”). The verb {lk 6:24 ἀπέχετε} is a commercial term for “paid in full”, used on receipts: the rich have already collected their comfort. Matthew uses the same verb for the hypocrites who {mt 6:2 ἀπέχουσιν τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν}.

The salt saying survives in three different settings, a good example of how individual sayings traveled. Matthew and Luke share the unusual verb {mt 5:13 μωρανθῇ} (*mōranthē*, literally “becomes foolish”), where Mark has {mk 9:50 ἄναλον γένηται} (“becomes saltless”). The odd word may reflect an Aramaic pun, since a similar root can mean both “tasteless” and “foolish”.

Matthew's Jesus insists that not one {mt 5:18 ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία} (“one iota or one serif”) will pass from the Law. Iota is the smallest Greek letter, and the *keraia* (“little horn”) is the tiny stroke that distinguishes similar Hebrew letters. Luke has the same saying in a different context and phrasing, but with the same unusual word {lk 16:17 κεραίαν}.

The first of Matthew's six “antitheses” (“you have heard… but **I** say to you”, {mt 5:22 ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν}). It contains the Aramaic insult {mt 5:22 Ῥακά} (*raka*, “empty-head”) left untranslated. The closing advice about settling with an accuser on the way to court also appears in Luke 12, but there it is about reading the signs of the times.

Only Matthew has this antithesis, which moves the commandment from act to intention: whoever looks {mt 5:28 πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν} (“in order to desire her”) has already committed adultery in his heart. The verb *epithymeō* is the one the Septuagint uses in the tenth commandment, “you shall not covet”, so the saying ties the seventh commandment to the tenth.

Luke's form is absolute: divorcing and remarrying is adultery. Matthew adds an exception, {mt 5:32 παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας} (“except on the ground of *porneia*”, sexual immorality), and adds a similar exception in his Mark-based divorce debate (19:9). Since neither Mark nor Luke has it, most scholars consider it Matthew's adaptation for his community. Paul also cites a no-divorce command from the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:10).

Only Matthew has the prohibition {mt 5:34 μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως} (“do not swear at all”). Compare the doubled simple words {mt 5:37 ναὶ ναί οὒ οὔ} (“yes, yes; no, no”). Nearly the same saying appears in the Letter of James (5:12), which shares several echoes of the Sermon on the Mount without quoting a Gospel.

Both open with the identical command {lk 6:27 ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν} (“love your enemies”), but the climax differs. Matthew's is {mt 5:48 τέλειοι} (“be **perfect/complete**, as your heavenly Father is”), Luke's {lk 6:36 οἰκτίρμονες} (“be **merciful**, as your Father is”). Matthew places the Golden Rule later, at 7:12, and adds {mt 7:12 οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται}, “this is the Law and the Prophets”.

First of three parallel warnings in Matthew (giving, prayer, fasting) built on the same pattern: don't perform piety {mt 6:2 ὥσπερ οἱ ὑποκριταὶ} (“as the hypocrites do”). *Hypokritēs* originally meant a stage actor. Matthew uses the word about thirteen times, more than any other Gospel. The image {mt 6:3 μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀριστερά σου τί ποιεῖ ἡ δεξιά σου} is unique to Matthew.

Matthew's version is longer and liturgical, with {mt 6:9 Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς} (“our Father in the heavens”); Luke's starts with just {lk 11:2 Πάτερ} (“Father”). Matthew prays for forgiveness of {mt 6:12 τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν} (“our **debts**”). Luke says {lk 11:4 τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν} (“our sins”) but keeps the debt image in the second half: {lk 11:4 παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν} (“everyone who **owes** us”). That suggests “debts” is the older wording.

The third of Matthew's piety warnings: when you fast, {mt 6:17 ἄλειψαί σου τὴν κεφαλὴν} (“anoint your head”), that is, look as you normally do. Mark and Luke record debates over **whether** Jesus' disciples fasted. Matthew alone gives instructions on **how** to fast, a sign that the practice continued in his community, as it did in the early church generally.

The closing line is almost identical in both, except for the number. Matthew uses {mt 6:21 ὁ θησαυρός σου} (“your”, singular), addressing each listener; Luke uses {lk 12:34 ὁ θησαυρὸς ὑμῶν} (“your”, plural), addressing the group. Luke sets the saying after a command Matthew lacks: “sell your possessions and give alms”, typical of Luke's sharper teaching on wealth.

Ancient optics often treated the eye as a lamp that sends out light. A {mt 6:22 ἁπλοῦς} (*haplous*) eye is literally “single” or “simple”, but in Jewish moral idiom it meant **generous**, while an “evil eye” meant stinginess. That explains why Matthew places this saying between teachings about treasure and money.

The highest agreement anywhere in the double tradition: 26 identical words in a row. Luke adds just one word, {lk 16:13 οἰκέτης} (“household slave”). Both keep the Aramaic {mt 6:24 μαμωνᾷ} (*mamōnas*, “wealth”) untranslated. Agreement this close is the kind of evidence that persuades most scholars that Matthew and Luke had a **written** common source (or that one copied the other).

Close agreement, but with telling differences. Matthew's {mt 6:26 τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ} (“birds of the sky”) are fed by {mt 6:26 ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος} (“your heavenly Father”); Luke's {lk 12:24 τοὺς κόρακας} (“ravens”, unclean birds under the Law) are fed by God. Matthew adds {mt 6:33 πρῶτον} (“seek **first**”) and {mt 6:33 τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ} (“and his righteousness”); righteousness is one of his favorite words.

The speck-and-beam saying is nearly verbatim in Matthew and Luke, a 14-word run. The comic image is built from {mt 7:3 τὸ κάρφος} (*karphos*, “a speck, a bit of straw”) against {mt 7:3 δοκὸν} (*dokos*, “a roof beam”). Luke places it in the shorter Sermon on the Plain, together with sayings about the blind leading the blind that Matthew uses elsewhere (15:14).

A cryptic saying found only in Matthew: {mt 7:6 Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσίν} (“do not give what is holy to dogs”), likely an image drawn from temple sacrifices. The Didache, an early Christian manual, applies it to keeping the Eucharist from the unbaptized. Its meaning in the Sermon itself is debated.

Matthew and Luke agree for 24 words in a row, then diverge at the punchline. Matthew's Father gives {mt 7:11 ἀγαθὰ} (“good things”), but Luke's gives {lk 11:13 πνεῦμα ἅγιον} (“the Holy Spirit”). Luke emphasizes the Spirit throughout his Gospel and Acts, so most scholars think “good things” is earlier and Luke has made the change.

Matthew contrasts two gates and two roads, {mt 7:13 διὰ τῆς στενῆς πύλης} (“through the narrow **gate**”), a teaching device also found in Jewish wisdom literature. Luke has a narrow **door** of a house about to be shut: {lk 13:24 Ἀγωνίζεσθε εἰσελθεῖν διὰ τῆς στενῆς θύρας} (“**strive** to enter by the narrow door”). The verb *agōnizesthe* comes from athletic contests.

The same proverb with the produce shuffled. Matthew: {mt 7:16 μήτι συλλέγουσιν ἀπὸ ἀκανθῶν σταφυλὰς ἢ ἀπὸ τριβόλων σῦκα} (grapes from thorns, figs from thistles). Luke: {lk 6:44 ἐξ ἀκανθῶν συλλέγουσιν σῦκα} (figs from thorns, grapes from brambles). Matthew aims the saying at false prophets; Luke makes it about the heart and speech.

Luke's version is a single pointed question: {lk 6:46 Τί δέ με καλεῖτε Κύριε κύριε καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω} (“why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord’ and not do what I say?”). Matthew expands it into a scene of the last judgment, where some who performed miracles in Jesus' name are rejected because they did not do {mt 7:21 τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου} (“the will of my Father”).

Both sermons end with this parable, strong evidence that Matthew's and Luke's sermons share a common framework. Matthew's builder is {mt 7:24 ἀνδρὶ φρονίμῳ} (“a sensible man”) who builds on rock, which fits Palestinian wadis that flood in winter. Luke's builder {lk 6:48 ἔσκαψεν καὶ ἐβάθυνεν} (“dug and went deep”) to lay a foundation, more like Greco-Roman construction.
